answers.answer: Open the latest stable release on GitHub. Download the archive whose ending matches your computer from the table: win-x64.zip for Windows, linux-x64.tar.gz or linux-arm64.tar.gz for Linux, osx-x64.tar.gz or osx-arm64.tar.gz for a Mac. On Windows, right-click the zip, choose Extract All, open the extracted folder and then the program folder inside it, and double-click nomnomz.exe. On Linux or macOS, open a terminal in the folder with the archive and run tar -xzf, cd and ./nomnomz. No browser opens by itself. On Windows, right-click the tray icon and choose Open in browser. On Linux or macOS, type http://localhost:5080, or the port from the startup message. The data lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\NomNomzBot on Windows, ~/.local/share/NomNomzBot on Linux and ~/Library/Application Support/NomNomzBot on macOS. To back it up, stop the bot and copy that whole folder.
answers.quote: Open the latest release on GitHub and download the archive for your computer.

answers.answer: The What you need section lists what you need first: a 64-bit Windows, Linux or macOS computer, a Twitch account for the channel, and a free port 5080. If you want a different port or a different data folder, you have to set it before the first start. Both of these are stated in the What you need section.
answers.quote: The bot makes its data folder the first time it starts, so set the folder first, as Choose another data folder shows.

answers.answer: The bot is running when the setup page opens in the browser. On Windows, the tray icon also appears with a notice that gives the address. On Linux and macOS, the terminal prints a startup message such as Listening on 5080.
answers.quote: When the setup page opens in your browser, the bot is running.

answers.answer: Before the first start, set NOMNOMZ_DATA_DIR to the folder on the second drive. On Windows, use setx in PowerShell, close PowerShell and double-click nomnomz.exe. On Linux or macOS, put the variable in front of ./nomnomz every time, or export it in the shell startup file. The variable must stay set, because without it the bot goes back to the default folder. The port the bot gets on its first start is written to listen-port in the data folder and reused on every later start, because the Twitch sign-in addresses include it. If another program holds that port later, the bot does not start.
answers.quote: Whatever port the bot gets on its first start, it keeps on every later start.

answers.answer: What you need says port 5080 must be free and that no other program may use it. Only later, under The bot keeps its port, do you learn that on the first start the bot simply takes another free port. I reread the two to check they agree; they do, but it costs a moment's doubt. Under When port 5080 is taken, the page tells you to close the program that uses the port but does not say how to find that program. A newcomer would have to look that up elsewhere.
answers.quote: The bot listens on port 5080, and no other program may use that port.

answers.answer: Read aloud, the sentence that spells out the reserved-port message piece by piece is hard to follow, and the listener has to rebuild the message in their head. The troubleshooting section also points to When port 5080 is taken twice in a row, which sounds repetitive when spoken.
answers.quote: It begins with Port, then that number, then is reserved for this bot.

The 355 words before step 1 are the access requirements (64-bit computer, Twitch account, free port 5080), the archive choice and the data-folder decision. Voice.md item 4 puts requirements that affect the steps before the steps, and the reader answered questions 1 and 2 from this text.

The reader picks the correct archive from it, so the sentence count does not hurt comprehension.

This is the late-start port paragraph: about five sentences covering the trigger (the bot does not start), where to read the port on Windows, what the Linux/macOS message says, and the fix. Each sentence gives one fact the reader needs at that moment. The spoken awkwardness of the reserved-port sentence is a wording nit, not a defect that stops a newcomer, because the message text can be matched on screen.
